articles.title: Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: Pre-Experiment Stage
articles.author: Widad Machmouchi, Somit Gupta, Ruhan Zhang, Aleksander Fabijan
articles.access_notes: Fetched via the group path /research/group/experimentation-platform-exp/articles/...; the listing page gives the /research/articles/ form used here. Read via WebFetch, so text came through a summarizer; no verbatim quotes used.
sections_read: Forming a hypothesis and selecting users

findings.summary: Keep each hypothesis simple and falsifiable with the metrics chosen; split a compound change into parts with their own hypotheses. A claim with no metric that could disprove it fails.
findings.section: Formulate the hypothesis and success metrics
findings.limitations: No worked numbers.

findings.summary: Every test carries a standard metric set (satisfaction, guardrail, feature/engagement, data quality), and a power calculation sets the minimum number of affected units before traffic is allocated.
findings.section: Formulate the hypothesis and success metrics
findings.limitations: No power or sample-size values given.

findings.summary: Check for pre-period bias: compare arms on the same metric in the period before the test (retrospective A/A). A significant pre-period gap makes a borderline in-test result suspect. It is an indicator, not proof.
findings.section: Check and account for pre-experiment bias
findings.limitations: Needs per-unit history for the same units; seed search over a couple hundred seeds is Microsoft-scale tooling.

findings.summary: When only some users can be affected, log in control which users would have been affected (counterfactual logging) so the comparison is like-for-like; verify it with SRM.
findings.limitations: Requires engineering control of both arms; Bing weather example only.

findings.summary: Microsoft News: a configuration error removed the search box from both variants of a custom control; it showed only when compared with a standard control that ran no experiment code.
findings.section: Use both a custom control and a standard control
findings.limitations: Single case; standard control costs traffic a small business does not have.

findings.summary: Ramp exposure in steps (example 1%, 5%, 10%, then target) and compute metrics at each step; start with dogfood/beta users but treat their result as a milestone, not proof.
findings.limitations: At low traffic a 1% stage has almost no power; only the safety purpose transfers.

articles.title: Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: During-Experiment Stage
articles.author: Widad Machmouchi, Somit Gupta, Ruhan Zhang
articles.access_notes: Full page read via WebFetch. A second URL (?p=720145) resolved to the same article.
sections_read: Monitor metrics to intervene when needed
Slice the analysis with appropriate segments

findings.summary: Four metric types per test: data quality (incl. SRM), OEC/goal, local feature/diagnostic, guardrail (things that must not get worse, e.g. load time, crashes, abandonment).
findings.section: Capture unexpected effects early with a complete metric set
findings.limitations: Examples are product telemetry, not small-business funnels.

findings.summary: Measure a small critical set early and often, but early looks need stricter significance; without very clear movement, wait for the planned end and read the result then.
findings.limitations: No stated early-look alpha.

findings.summary: Alert on guardrails and goal metrics using a large movement, a low p-value, or both; alert on SRM early because it usually invalidates the test; auto-stop tests that badly hurt users.
findings.limitations: No numeric thresholds in this article.

findings.summary: A Bing test with a bug served a 404 page; automatic shutdown limited the harm.
findings.limitations: Anecdote; no magnitudes.

findings.summary: Use segments the treatment cannot change (country, browser, pre-test activity). If the whole test has no SRM, each static segment should also be SRM-free; dynamic segments (e.g. activity buckets) can shift under treatment.
findings.section: Use segments that are stable during the test
findings.limitations: Per-segment SRM needs volume per segment.

findings.summary: Microsoft News swapped a button and saw a 28% rise in clicks, but a by-date view showed clicks falling day over day (novelty), and the change did not ship. Segment every analysis by date: steady decline suggests novelty; a one-day spike suggests a data problem or a one-off event.
findings.limitations: Daily granularity assumes enough daily volume; small businesses may need weekly buckets.

articles.title: Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: Post-Experiment Stage
articles.author: Widad Machmouchi, Somit Gupta
articles.access_notes: Not linked from the during-experiment article; found by search and the listing page 2.
sections_read: Verify treatment effects do not invalidate metrics
Estimate the final impact of the treatment
Close the loop on experiment results

findings.summary: Before reading behaviour metrics, confirm the setup: counts match the allocation, everyone in the analysis is in the target audience, and the movements the change must cause (e.g. coverage of a new element) actually appear.
findings.section: Ensure metric movements align with the test set-up
findings.limitations: Checklist, no thresholds.

findings.summary: Skype: treatment improved call-logging reliability and control did not, so metric movements reflected logging, not behaviour. Compute data-quality metrics on every test to catch telemetry changes that differ by arm.
findings.limitations: Single case.

findings.summary: Metric-level SRM: in an MSN test treatment drove more homepage loads, the extra loads were slow, and page load time looked worse. A test-level SRM pass does not clear each metric's denominator.
findings.section: Check for imbalance in metric observation units
findings.limitations: Detection method described qualitatively.

findings.summary: Triggered analysis (only users the change could affect) gains sensitivity but needs full recall of affected users, no SRM in the triggered set, and a flat triggered-complement; the triggered effect must then be diluted by the trigger rate before claiming a site-wide impact.
findings.section: Segment by triggered users / Dilute gains
findings.limitations: Ratio-metric dilution needs a regression method the article only cites.

findings.summary: Clear ship: goal up (or flat in a well-powered test) and guardrails neutral or better. Mixed results (goal up, guardrail down) need trade-off weights set in advance from business direction, not per test.
findings.limitations: No standard weights.

findings.summary: Bing: a low-engagement filter change showed a surprising significant satisfaction gain; a re-randomized rerun with more traffic was flat. Surprising results should be reproduced before acting; archive hypotheses and results for later meta-analysis.
findings.section: When in doubt, reproduce results / Archive
findings.limitations: Rerun cost is low at Bing scale; for a small business a rerun can take months.

articles.title: Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in A/B Testing
articles.author: Aleksander Fabijan, Vaibhav Kumar Bajpai, Trevor Blanarik, Max Caughron, Kewei Chen, Ruhan Zhang, Adam Gustafson, Venkata Kavitha Budumuri, Stephen Hunt
articles.access_notes: Fetched via the group path; the listing gives the /research/articles/ form. No numeric chi-square worked example in the article.

findings.summary: About 6% of Microsoft A/B tests have an SRM; LinkedIn reported about 10% of triggered (zoomed-in) tests affected.
findings.limitations: Platform-specific rates; a small business with hand-built splits may see more.

findings.summary: Every Microsoft test must pass a chi-square SRM check on raw unit counts before any effect is read; ExP flags at p < 0.0005, chosen to limit false alarms, noting real SRMs are usually far below it.
findings.limitations: Threshold tuned for thousands of tests a year; at a few hundred units a real skew can sit above it.

findings.summary: Cause taxonomy by stage: assignment (bucketing, bad IDs, carry-over), execution (redirects in one arm, treatment changing engagement), log processing (joins), analysis (biased trigger or segment conditions), plus uneven ramping or self-selection into an arm.
findings.limitations: From the authors' KDD 2019 paper; summarized only.

findings.summary: Diagnosis: is the SRM local to a segment or everywhere; does it vanish in the untriggered population (then the trigger is at fault); when did it start; how extreme is the p-value; which arm has extra units (extra treatment units often mean better engagement or filtering); are many tests affected at once (pipeline).
findings.limitations: The 'when did it start' analysis was deferred to a later post.

findings.summary: MSN carousel (12 vs 16 cards): engaged treatment users tripped a bot filter and were dropped, which looked like an engagement loss and failed SRM; after the fix the variant was positive.
findings.limitations: No counts given.

articles.title: Alerting in Microsoft's Experimentation Platform (ExP)
articles.author: Ankita Agrawal, Vaibhav Kumar Bajpai, Jiannan Lu
articles.access_notes: Read via WebFetch; ?p=729247 is the same article.

findings.summary: Two main alerts: SRM (chi-square on randomization-unit counts) and metric out of range, built as an equivalence test against experimenter-set absolute and relative bounds using two one-sided tests.
findings.limitations: Equivalence tests need volume to show a metric is inside a bound; small samples can only show a breach.

findings.summary: Bounds come from domain knowledge, heuristics and history and differ by metric (a few ms of load time ignored; a 0.1% move in a reliability metric can matter). Example: a Bing click-rate alert fires on a 5% or larger drop.
findings.limitations: Bounds are product-specific.

findings.summary: Many tests, analysis windows and metrics require multiple-testing control; ExP uses Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate.
findings.limitations: With one primary and two or three guardrails, BH matters little; tiered bounds matter more.

findings.summary: Alerts go by email with priority P0 (catastrophic), P1 (serious), P2 (possibly wrong); owners can resolve or suppress recurring false alarms; auto-shutdown for some time-critical tests.
findings.limitations: Workflow sized for hundreds of alerts a year.

findings.summary: 2020: duplicate device IDs were fixed, but the treatment kept reading old IDs and gained extra users; an SRM alert days later led to the fix and a quick restart.
findings.limitations: No counts.

articles.title: p-Values for Your p-Values: Validating Metric Trustworthiness by Simulated A/A Tests
articles.author: Carl Mitchell, Andy Drake, Jonathan Litz, Garnet Vaz

findings.summary: Under a true null, p-values should be uniform (about 5% below 0.05). Simulate A/A tests offline by re-hashing historical logs with new seeds; about 100 simulations is usually enough (they ran 200), checked with Anderson-Darling.
findings.limitations: Needs per-unit historical logs.

findings.summary: One user with over a million duplicated clicks pins p-values near 0.32 because the outlier always sits in one arm; capping (e.g. clicks at 50) restores uniformity and sensitivity.
findings.limitations: Click-stream example.

findings.summary: Rare-event metrics are unreliable: with 15 users there are only 8 possible splits (15-0 to 8-7), so only 8 distinct p-values exist. Constant metrics give no information.
findings.limitations: Directly relevant to small businesses; no general minimum given.

findings.summary: Across about a dozen products, 10% to 15% of metrics typically failed the uniformity check, up to 30% in some; checks must repeat because outliers appear over time.
findings.limitations: July 2020 Microsoft data.

articles.title: Beyond Power Analysis: Metric Sensitivity Analysis in A/B Tests
articles.author: Wen Qin, Widad Machmouchi, Alexandre Matos Martins
articles.access_notes: Read alongside the related 'STEDII Properties of a Good Metric' (2022-04-06, Gupta and Machmouchi), which repeats the sensitivity decomposition; STEDII is not listed separately.

findings.summary: Sensitivity = how often the metric really moves (movement probability) times power. A well-powered metric that rarely moves gives few usable results; a null on such a metric says little.
findings.limitations: Movement probability is estimated from a corpus of past tests, which a small business lacks.

findings.summary: Check the minimum detectable effect at typical traffic with the feature team: is a change that size realistic? Teams' Time in App could detect 0.3% with full traffic for a week, judged achievable, yet it still missed changes other metrics caught.
findings.limitations: Microsoft Teams scale.

findings.summary: Improve insensitive metrics: cap extremes, log-transform, use proportion metrics (easier to move), conditional averages, predictive proxies for slow goals, and CUPED with pre-period data. Keep hard-to-move top-level metrics as guardrails rather than success metrics (STEDII).
findings.limitations: CUPED gains depend on how much pre-period data explains (Deep Dive into Variance Reduction reports many metrics gaining little).

findings.summary: With a labelled corpus: sensitivity N1/(N1+N2) near 1, false-positive share N3/(N3+N4) near alpha; without labels, compare observed movement rates, trusting differences above 5 points.
findings.limitations: Needs many past tests.

articles.title: External Validity of Online Experiments: Can We Predict the Future?
articles.author: Not listed on the page (Microsoft Experimentation Platform group)
articles.access_notes: Author names not present in the fetched text.

findings.summary: Across 1,000+ experiments, adjacent-day effect differences match a normal curve up to about 3 standard errors but have far heavier tails beyond; a day's error bar overstates confidence about the next day.
findings.limitations: Large-sample average metrics only.

findings.summary: Going from 7 to 14 days shrank the standard error 83% of the time and grew it 17%; the 14-day estimate fell outside the 7-day 95% interval 9% of the time versus about 5% expected.
findings.limitations: Restricted to significant 7-day results; the 14-day value is a proxy, not truth.

findings.summary: Run at least a week, extend when effects are still changing, use holdouts or reverse tests to check persistence; novelty/primacy explain part of the drift, outside events the rest.
findings.limitations: The authors stress these problems are the exception.

concepts.name: Guardrails as pre-set harm bounds, with harm stops allowed
concepts.decision: Did the change cause harm that blocks shipping, and may the test stop early for it?
applies_when: any live test touching customers: email, offers, pricing, booking flow, ads
evidence_required: 1-3 guardrails each with a numeric bound written before launch
steps: At plan time: name guardrails with bounds (e.g. unsubscribe rate <= 1.0%, refunds <= 2 per 100 orders)
During test: check bounds weekly; a breach in treatment (with a minimum count) pauses the test: this is a harm stop, not peeking
At the end: goal up or flat and all guardrails within bounds -> ship-eligible; any breach -> no ship, or an explicit trade-off weighed in advance
Do not read a non-significant guardrail rise as 'safe'
alternatives: low traffic: absolute bounds with a minimum count instead of significance
no randomization: compare guardrail to the pre-period, labelled observed

stop_review: bound breached with minimum count met: pause and review

concepts.name: Pick a metric that can move; keep the outcome as a guardrail
concepts.decision: Which primary metric makes this test feasible inside the horizon?
applies_when: primary metric is a rare outcome (bookings, sales) at low traffic
avoid_when: the proxy has no plausible link to the outcome
proxy is easily gamed (clicks via bait)
evidence_required: baseline for the outcome and for the candidate proxy
steps: Size the outcome with sampleSize at its own baseline
If weeks exceed the horizon, size a nearer step (e.g. 'clicked Book now')
Use the proxy as primary, keep bookings as a guardrail/secondary read
Count only units the change can reach (triggered), and dilute by reach rate before claiming site-wide impact
If the proxy is still infeasible: before/after or qualitative path
alternatives: low traffic: one bigger change, longer window, or interviews
no randomization: before/after on the proxy, labelled observed
no instrumentation: manual counts of booking clicks for 2 weeks
concepts.observation_window: Whole weeks from sampleSize, within the plan horizon.
stop_review: proxy up but outcome down: no ship

triggered example: a 10% relative lift among the 20% of visitors who reach pricing is about 2% site-wide (0.20 x 10%)

reports the triggered 10% lift as site-wide

concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: size feasibility with the primary metric's baseline when known; suggest the nearest feasible funnel step otherwise.

concepts.name: Small-business A/A: a dry run of the split, not a p-value study
concepts.decision: Is the owner's split mechanism trustworthy before the first real test?
applies_when: first owner-built split (two email lists, alternating landing pages, staff assigning leads)
avoid_when: platform-native split tools with proven assignment and exposed counts (still run the SRM check)
evidence_required: one week of both arms identical
prerequisites: the same tracking in both arms
steps: Run both arms identical for 7 days
sampleRatio passes (not warn)
Every event type appears in both arms; no unit in both arms
Do not judge conversion p-values: rare events give few possible outcomes
If unit-level history exists (e.g. an email list with past opens), ClimbOS can re-randomize it offline about 100 times in code and check that about 5% fall below 0.05
alternatives: no instrumentation: fix tracking first (diagnostics 'tracking' verdict)
guardrails: no customer-visible difference during the dry run
stop_review: SRM warn or missing events: fix before any real test

expected_behavior: SRM chi-square 2.25, p = 0.1336: split passes
form_start missing in treatment: dry run fails on event parity
no conversion-rate verdict
hard_failure: passes the dry run because SRM passed
reports an A/A conversion p-value as proof the system works

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: ExP's A/A is a statistical calibration on large logs; at small scale, its trust-check purpose (assignment and telemetry parity) transfers, its p-value calibration mostly does not.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: recommend a 7-day dry run before an owner's first manual split; pass = SRM pass + event parity.
